doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Quitting and rejoining Flanagan, then Jack Teagarden at the Meadowbrook
summary: After the tour he quit, rejoined Flanagan a year later, and auditioned for Teagarden while Flanagan complained about his own band.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Quitting the band: why sidemen left

blocks.x: I expected much more. From then on I just got very — like I said when I came home I said — oh boy they all said, you know, starry eyed, and thought I’d be stage struck. “How was it?” “It was the fucking worst” I said. Plain and simple. It was the fucking worst. Ohhhh. They all wanted to do that. And I had done it. So I didn’t see any romance to that whatsoever. So I quit him for six months and re-joined him a year later. I was one of the only few guys to ever re-join him. You know, when you left that band, you left. And then I joined Jack Teagarden while I was still with Ralph at the Hotel New Yorker. And Jack was holding auditions out at the Meadowbrook. And at the Meadowbrook I joined up with him and Ralph, I remember walking in, and he let me take off it was a matinee and I came in about 7:30 after I got back from the Meadowbrook, they had a matinee there. So I came in and Ralph is conducting, and he looks at me and he sees me coming through and he says, “How did you make out?” And I says, “I made it.” He says, “They need a piano player?” I says, “You’ve got your own band.” He says, “this pile of shit?” Right from the bandstand he says, “this pile of shit” he says.
He was trying to get away from it.
Yeah. He wanted out of it. He wanted out of that band. He’d had it by then. But he was a marvelous guy in his own way.

A lot of guys were frightened to death of him. But he was a big money maker and it was a good band. We had section rehearsals and stuff, and a lot of guys didn’t like that kind of music, well neither did I but I was the hot clarinet player. I enjoyed the last 15 minutes, playing with a trio or quartet. That kept me together.
I was going to say, when you made a move to Jack Teagarden you’d have to play a lot more from your ears.

Yeah but that’s what I always wanted to do anyway. I had a lot of experience doing it, sitting in with other bands. I mean before I went on the road with a mickey band so to speak, I was always — I learned the repertoire thoroughly, all the harmony parts, all the what have you. So it wasn’t like I was stepping into something that was foreign territory to me.
